source: Diamond et al. (2010) The promise of a cognitive perspective on jury deliberation, Psychonomic Bulletin & Review 17(2):174-
finding: Gap 2. The Kalven and Zeisel first-ballot figure is a retrospective juror report, not a measured first vote. First-ballot majority matched the verdict in 90% of cases, but Kalven and Zeisel themselves called it a 'radical hunch'.
numbers: 225 jurors' retrospective reports; majority on first ballot predicted verdict in 90% of cases (Kalven & Zeisel 1966, from a survey of about 3,500 criminal trials by judge reports).
quote: Because a majority vote on the first ballot predicted the jury's verdict in 90% of the cases
limits: Secondary source: Kalven & Zeisel original not opened. The 225-juror subset is as described by Diamond et al.
agent_relevance: Do not use '90% decided on the first vote' as evidence that deliberation (or a second pass) adds nothing. It is a weak, self-reported figure.

finding: Gap 2. Why the 90% figure understates deliberation: real juries often do not take an immediate anonymous vote, and a vote taken after discussion hides earlier movement.
numbers: Immediate first votes: 21% of juries (Diamond & Casper 1992), 28% (Hastie, Penrod & Pennington 1983); real-juror surveys 3% (Sandys & Dillehay 1995) to 31% (Devine et al. 2004). Arizona Filming Project: 50 civil cases, only 20% voted in first 10 minutes; delay in voting rose with trial length (r=.54). 38% of jurors rated leaning 3, 4 or 5 on a 7-point scale before deliberation (17% at midpoint 4). 20% of jurors in 382 criminal trials said they only leaned to a side during deliberation.
limits: Review; each cited study not opened. Juror self-report may be inflated by the court's instruction not to decide early.
agent_relevance: In our agent, record the true first answer before any critique step. Real juries do not, so 'first answer wins' rates from them are biased upward.

source: Diamond et al. (2010) citing Devine et al. (2001) and Davis et al. (1975) (hung juries, thresholds)
finding: Gap 2. Lab jury simulations show high hung rates and a conviction threshold above two thirds; real hung rate is under 10%.
numbers: Devine et al. 2001 review: when no more than three fourths of initial preferences favoured a verdict, 31% hung. Hung rate across all lab studies 21% vs under 10% outside the lab. Conviction threshold 'somewhat higher than two thirds'. Davis et al. 1975 best model: two thirds initial majority wins, else hang. Real juries: 85% of hung juries had at least 3 jurors disagreeing with majority (382 criminal trials). Judge sided with majority 8 times (57%) and holdouts 6 times (42%) in a non-unanimous jurisdiction (Diamond, Rose & Murphy 2006).
limits: Devine et al. 2001 itself still not opened; these are Diamond et al.'s quotes of it. Lab deliberations are time-capped, inflating hung rates.
agent_relevance: Hung outcomes in LLM mock juries (Ersoz 17 of 18) should be compared with lab, not real, base rates, and lab rates are themselves inflated by time limits.

source: Bessis, Wills, Wojciechowski, White & Pothos (2026) Legal Decision Biases in GPT: A Comparison with Human Judgment, Behavioral Sciences 16(3):437
finding: Gap 1 (nearest found). First LLM test of evidence-order effects on a legal verdict rating: GPT-4o and GPT-5.2 rated guilt higher when incriminating evidence came last (recency), and an intermediate guilt rating shifted final ratings. It manipulates incriminating versus exonerating order, not story versus source order.
numbers: Six simplified criminal cases, N=720 trials per model per prompt condition, temperature 1. GPT-4o baseline: order main effect F(1,711)=424.76, p<.001; rating-condition F(1,711)=181.11; order x rating F(1,711)=43.75. GPT-5.2 baseline: order F(1,711)=71.24, p<.001 (smaller); rating condition F(1,711)=8.43, p=.0038. Combined agents: order F(1,2138)=205.09. Rerun at T=0.2: case-level means correlate r=.996 (GPT-4o) and r=.989 (GPT-5.2).
quote: GPT-4o exhibited robust order effects and a form of evaluation bias
limits: Guilt on a rating scale, no story structure manipulated. Per-cell means in the PDF text are garbled, so only the F values are recorded here. Human data from Wojciechowski et al. (2025), not opened.
agent_relevance: Order sensitivity is real in current models, so the agent should be run on 2+ evidence orders and flips treated as low confidence. A story-versus-source order test is still not done.

finding: Prompting did not remove order or evaluation bias in GPT-5.2; careful-reasoning-plus-justify made order worse.
numbers: Four system prompts x 720 trials (2,880 per model): PE0 baseline, PE1 legal-expert persona with impartiality, PE2 'reason carefully', PE3 reason carefully and be ready to justify with case elements. GPT-5.2 order effect remained significant in all (F(1,2859)=574.40); PE1 beta=0.03 p=.62, PE2 beta=0.07 p=.28, PE3 beta=0.39 SE=0.07 p<.0001 (bigger than baseline). Evaluation bias rose under PE1 (beta=0.16, p=.018) and PE3 (beta=0.23, p<.001).
limits: No chain-of-thought arm by design. Only two OpenAI models. Authors call the prompts illustrative.
agent_relevance: Asking the agent to justify from the case (a story-like step) can raise order sensitivity. Use structural controls (re-run under permuted order), not instructions.

source: Liu, Tong et al. (2025) Legal Fact Prediction: The Missing Piece in Legal Judgment Prediction, EMNLP 2025
finding: Gap 1. LLMs predicting civil judgments from evidence lists favour the party whose evidence is listed last.
numbers: LFPBench: 657 Chinese civil cases, 10 case types. Finding 7: with plaintiff evidence last, models predict more complete or partial plaintiff wins; with defendant evidence last, plaintiff loss rate rises. Six LLMs tested (GPT-4o, Claude 3.5, Qwen2.5-14B, Llama-based legal models). Example in Table 8: GPT-4o accuracy 42.19 (defendant first, plaintiff last) vs 48.80 (plaintiff first).
limits: Table 8 text is garbled in extraction, so row-to-model alignment of the numbers is uncertain; only the direction (recency) is relied on. No story-order condition.
agent_relevance: Another independent LLM recency result, in a real-case benchmark. Supports permuted-order checks.

source: Kumaran et al. (2025) How Overconfidence in Initial Choices and Underconfidence Under Criticism Modulate Change of Mind in LLMs (Google DeepMind/UCL)
finding: Gap 8 (analog). LLMs show a choice-supportive bias: seeing their own earlier answer raises their confidence in it and cuts changes of mind. This is a coherence-shift-like effect, measured on confidence, not on evidence ratings.
numbers: Two-turn latitude-of-cities binary choice, Gemma 3 12B (2,000 questions x 36 conditions), also Gemma 3 27B, GPT-4o, o1-preview. Mean change-of-mind rate 32.5% when answer hidden vs 13.1% when shown (p=0.002; display coefficient -3.4, p<0.0001). Opposite advice: 39.2% shown vs 85.0% hidden. Opposing advice overweighted vs ideal Bayesian; consistent advice not significantly overweighted.
limits: Not legal and not about rating evidence. Binary geography questions, calibrated by temperature scaling (T=3.3). Paper is a preprint.
agent_relevance: Showing the agent its own candidate before it rates evidence or confidence will inflate support for that candidate. Rate evidence blind to the candidate first.

source: Dutta & Moharir (2026) Stability vs. Manipulability: Evaluating Robustness Under Post-Decision Interaction in LLM Judges
finding: Gap 8/9 (analog). Judge verdicts are stable under neutral re-asking but reverse under targeted challenge, with low-overlap justifications that look like rationalisation.
numbers: MT-Bench and AlpacaEval. Anti-baseline challenge reverses 49% of decisions; counterbalanced persuasion susceptibility PS=0.194 (19.4%); net directional steering signed DS=-0.018 (clipped 0); 64% of reversals harmful; authority framing most destabilising.
limits: Preprint, LLM-as-judge on chat quality, not law or evidence rating. Model list not recorded here.
agent_relevance: A flip after challenge is mostly reversibility, not learning. Gate flips on new evidence or a code check, not on an argued challenge.

source: Ersoz (2026) 12 Angry AI Agents (full-text re-read for design)
finding: Gap 5. Full text shows the cause of 17/18 hung runs cannot be assigned: temperature was fixed, only two models, and the persona stays in the no-vote condition.
numbers: Temperature 0.9, max 150 turns, N=3 per cell, 18 runs. GPT-4o mean vote changes 1.0 (baseline), 0.7 (no initial vote), 1.0 (open-minded). Llama-4-Scout 2.0, 3.3, 6.0 (runs 5, 5, 8). Single non-hung run: Llama no-initial-vote, NOT_GUILTY after 64 turns. Authors state persona consistency may itself contribute to anchoring.
limits: No temperature sweep, no persona-free arm, two models only; RLHF intensity is confounded with model family, size and vendor. Gap 5 stays open.
agent_relevance: Do not rely on 'LLM juries never move' as a base rate. Use it only to say that persona-seeded panels barely deliberate.

source: Bertalanic & Fortuna (2026) The Cost of Consensus (full-text check of per-cell values)
finding: Gap 7 closed. Per-cell values confirmed: on GSM-Hard, Ministral-3-8B debate 20.7% vs self-correction 48.3% vs zero-shot 24.7%.
numbers: Ministral GSM-Hard debate 20.7% vs self-correction 48.3% (p<0.001); tokens per problem 23,816 vs 10,707. Ministral MMLU-Hard: self-correction 65.3% vs debate 62.0% (p=0.002). Llama-3.1-8B: 47.7% vs 45.0%, p=0.131 (not significant); GSM-Hard debate 39.3%. Modal sycophancy up to 85.5% (Qwen MMLU-Hard); oracle gap 32.3 points (Ministral GSM-Hard, oracle team 53.0%).
limits: Small open models (7-8B), three rounds, N=10 agents. Llama differences were not significant, so the headline case is Ministral only.
agent_relevance: Debate as a stand-in for deliberation is costly and can destroy accuracy in weak models. Self-check at half the tokens was better here.

source: Kumarappan & Mujoo (2026) Not Just RLHF (full-text check of cell values)
finding: Gap 7 closed. Yield under fake consensus depends on where the consensus is placed and on a single dissenter.
numbers: User-role framing: yield below 13% for 0 to 3 wrong peers, 80.25% at 4v0, 12.75% at 3v1. Assistant-role framing: below 7% for 0 to 2, 60.25% at 3v1, 97.50% at 4v0. Cross-framing gap at 3v1 = 47.5 points. N=5 jurors: 80.50% at cliff vs 20.00% below it. Dissenter cut at the cliff: 67.50 pp (N=4).
limits: Factual QA with injected peer answers, not deliberation on evidence. Authors flag a 12-point suffix effect (80.25 vs 68.00 unsuffixed).
agent_relevance: A protected dissent slot is cheap and measured to cut yield in this task. Not shown for evidence-weighing tasks.

source: Hao et al. (2026) Not All Flips Are Conformity (full-text check)
finding: Gap 7 closed. Full-reasoning debate gives no net majority-vote gain over self-reflection and costs 57% more tokens.
numbers: 4,900 questions (1,040 with initial disagreement, 5,200 agent-question pairs). Majority-vote accuracy 76.22% (round 0), 77.18% (stance-only), 77.35% (self-reflection) and 77.35% (full reasoning). Individual accuracy 36.88% to 42.17% (self-reflection), 44.48% (stance only), 45.87% (full reasoning). Paired difference 0.00 pp, 95% CI [-0.59, +0.59]. Majority transitions: 130 newly correct vs 75 newly wrong (self-reflection); 107 each (reasoning vs self-reflection). Tokens 4,469 vs 7,019.
limits: Preprint, QA benchmarks with small open models. Individual gains can come from ensemble effects.
agent_relevance: Count majority accuracy, not individual flips, when scoring any panel step. Equal-token baseline: self-reflection.

source: Hu, Shen & Lakshmipathi (2026) Statistical Scouting Finds Debate-Safe but Not Debate-Useful Cases: A Matched-Ceiling Study
finding: Gap 9. At a matched 960-token generation ceiling, no protocol wins everywhere, and cheap signals recover little of the routing gain. Neither protected dissent nor a code-triggered recheck was tested.
numbers: MuSiQue and GSM8K, Llama 3.1 8B and Ministral 3 8B; greedy vs 3-sample vote vs two-agent critique-revise debate. Oracle protocol choice adds +14.0 and +13.7 pp on MuSiQue. Each of four model-dataset cells has a different best protocol; debate leads only for Llama on MuSiQue. Vote-entropy escalation: +1.3 pp (Llama), +1.7 pp (Ministral); Fisher combined p=0.22; combined +1.6 pp p=0.125.
limits: Ceiling, not realised tokens (debate uses more). Small models. Gains are not significant.
agent_relevance: A code-triggered recheck on vote disagreement is the only gating rule with a positive trend, and weak. Protected dissent vs recheck stays untested.

source: Zhu, Zhang et al. (2026) Demystifying Multi-Agent Debate: The Role of Confidence and Diversity
finding: Gap 9. Vanilla debate often fails to beat majority vote; two fixes (diverse starting answers, confidence-modulated updates) are reported to beat vanilla debate and majority vote on six QA benchmarks.
numbers: Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, six reasoning QA benchmarks (read abstract and method; table values not extracted). Claim: both interventions consistently outperform vanilla MAD and majority vote.
limits: Per-benchmark numbers not recorded. Not an equal-token comparison against a recheck. Small open models.
agent_relevance: Supports keeping dissenting starting views alive. Starting diversity matters more than the number of rounds.

source: Fox, Markham, Lail & Karotsieris (2026) LLM Judges Verify Presence, Not Absence: Omission Blindness in AI Clinical Notes
finding: Gap 3 (analog, non-legal). Listing what the source establishes, then checking each item as a closed present-or-absent question, recovers omission detection that wording changes, voting and prompt optimisation did not. It is a coverage check, not a story check.
numbers: 500 single-error note pairs (298 omissions, 202 added/altered controls). Paired discrimination 0.79-0.94 on added/altered content vs 0.50-0.63 on omissions across 8 judge designs. Single-call evolved prompt detects 36.9% vs pipeline 24.6% of flawed notes (p=0.002), at 6.2% vs 2.7% false alarms, about a tenth of the cost. 25-item checklist 0.647 vs about 62-fact recipe 0.817 on the evaluation set.
limits: Clinical notes, judge task, not reasoning accuracy. Cost not at equal tokens to a baseline. Preprint from August 2026.
agent_relevance: Gaps in an account are caught by an explicit list-then-verify step, not by asking for 'is anything missing'. Supports the coverage check in the schema as a structure effect, not a story effect.

source: McKenzie, Lee & Chen (2002) When negative evidence increases confidence: change in belief after hearing two sides of a dispute, J. Behav. Decis. Making 15, DOI 10.1002/bdm.400
finding: Gap 10. Abstract-level only: four experiments found that a case judged weakly in favour of one side often raised confidence in the opposing side, and the reverse impact grew with the strength of the first case.
numbers: Exact cell values not available; paper behind a paywall and no full text found. Index abstracts seen through search results only.
limits: Not opened. Authors explain it with a demanding, malleable reference point, and say it reverses when the weak case is clearly unbiased. No LLM test found.
agent_relevance: A weak self-generated rival may strengthen the favoured answer. When the agent writes a rival hypothesis, score the rival's strength before showing it. Test with an LLM remains undone.

finding: Gap 4 and 6 stay open. Searches (3 web, OpenAlex, arXiv) found no replication of the story-versus-witness-order result with cell sizes, no failed replication, and no test of story form against a matched non-story structure. A dissertation (Reardon, FIU 2008) was reported in a search snippet as finding that the order effect reversed between student and community samples; the page returned 403 so this is not verified.
numbers: No numbers. Smith 1988 not located. Semantic Scholar and arXiv APIs returned 429 or empty.
limits: Absence in this search is not absence in the literature; paywalled journals were not reachable.
agent_relevance: Treat the story-order effect as single-study (Pennington & Hastie 1992) and run our own order test.
